fields.title: Polka: the feature reviewed in time
fields.summary: Referral program before development: 500 bonuses to both right after registration.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do we change before implementation? State the cost of your decision.
fields.brief/role: You are a Polka product manager.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a customer app, and a partner dashboard.
fields.brief/context: You are a Polka product manager. A referral program is planned: a customer invites a friend via a link, and both get 500 bonuses. Discovery is complete, design is ready, development starts in a week. Triage triggered on two flags: money and user interaction.
fields.brief/objective: Modify the program design so the budget doesn't drain on fake registrations.
fields.brief/constraints: Development starts in a week. Marketing budget is 3 million per quarter.
fields.brief/task: Decide what to change before implementation and justify the change.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Abuse is designed along with the feature
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Ask how to game your mechanics dishonestly, and the answer usually points to the moment you pay. Shifting the payout to an action that is expensive to fake neutralizes the main scheme in days. Limits and anomaly signals cover the rest, and dropping the idea is almost always disproportionate: the design works, not the ban.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: Link with an identifier, registration via it, crediting to both right after the invited user registers.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: 500 bonuses = 500 rubles, redeemable on orders of 1,500 or more.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: The referrer sees how many people came via their link. Invited names are not shown.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Launch as designed, monitor for abuse
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Launch as designed, monitor for abuse. Zero.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: with 11% fake in the past campaign and a simpler scheme here — likely more. The 3m budget can go to fake registrations. Post-factum detection, bonus clawback is conflict-heavy.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Credit after the invited user's first order
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Credit after the invited user's first order. Three days.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: fake registration stops being profitable — a real paid order is needed. Mechanics are slightly harder to explain. Program conversion is lower, but invited user quality is higher.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Credit after order plus limits plus monitoring
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Credit after order plus limits plus monitoring. One week.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: everything from B, plus a per-person invite limit, plus anomaly signals in the log. Closes mass schemes too.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Zero work. Drop the referral program and return 3 million to other acquisition channels.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: Abuse risk is zero, value too: a channel that works for competitors is simply left untried. Marketing returns 3 million to other channels with known and higher acquisition costs. Meanwhile, the abuse scheme is closed by changing the crediting moment in three days — dropping it is disproportionate to the found risk.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not conduct threat analysis before implementation
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Does not build an attacker model
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Does not embed verification into discovery
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Risk review is not embedded in discovery, done after design
